retrieval_text: A 76-year-old, right-handed, Caucasian female presented with significant gait impairment. She has a history of SS, evidenced by a decade of sicca symptoms, reduced tear production as shown by Schirmer's test, and the presence of anti-Ro/SS-A antibodies. Over the past 6 months, her gait rapidly worsened, leading to frequent falls and necessitating the use of a wheelchair for mobility outside her home.

The patient is a 13-year-old Japanese boy who was born at a normal weight of 2954 g. He presented with ectrodactyly in the right hand and left foot, along with syndactyly in both feet. Surgical correction was performed on the left foot at 1 year of age and on the right foot at 11 years of age, with no complications reported. Post-surgery, he is able to walk comfortably, and no further interventions are planned. Additionally, the patient exhibited dry skin and café au lait spots, as well as dental anomalies characterized by notched and narrower edges of the incisors, resulting in a peg-shaped appearance. There were no observations of cleft lip and palate, mammary gland hypoplasia, lachrymal duct atresia, or ankyloblepharon. The patient also has attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). There is no history of carcinomas in the patient or his parents.

An 8-year-old male from Cameroon presented at the Grace Community Health and Development Association outreach unit with progressive muscle contractures and weakness in the lower limbs, upper limbs, and trunk muscles over a period of 4 months. Initially, the weakness and contractures began in the lower limbs and within a month extended to the upper limbs and trunk muscles. This was characterized by flexural deformity of the elbow and ankle. The patient progressively experienced difficulty in walking or standing without support, poor head and waist control, and difficulty swallowing. There were no seizures, cognitive impairment, visual or auditory impairment, and no bladder or bowel dysfunction. A district hospital initially considered poliomyelitis, but stool samples tested negative for polio. His birth history was uneventful, with standing without support at 7 months and walking at 12 months. Other developmental milestones were normal, and he had normal motor and mental functions before the onset of symptoms. There was no history of measles, HIV, trauma, or hospitalization. He was fully vaccinated according to national guidelines. There was no family history of paralytic disease or mental impairment. Both parents are alive and well. On physical examination, the patient was conscious, afebrile, with no facial dimorphic features. Pupillary size and reflexes were normal. There was no ptosis or facial weakness. There was wasting of the upper limb, scapular, and spinal muscles, and contractures of the elbows and ankles. There was no calf hypertrophy or pseudohypertrophy. Muscle power was 4/5 in both upper and lower limbs. There was weakness in the cervical, lumbar, and pelvic muscles, evident by poor head control and swaying movements of the waist. Hypertonia was noted in the muscles of the arm and calf, with the upper limbs in a semi-flexed position. Sensitivity to touch, pain, temperature, vibration, and proprioception were preserved. Tendon and cutaneous reflexes were normal. He was unable to stand or walk without support. Gowers sign was absent. Cardiorespiratory examination revealed an irregularly irregular tachycardia with a heart rate of 122 beats per minute. There was no palpable abdominal mass or hepatosplenomegaly. The rest of the physical examinations were unremarkable.

A 30-year-old male presented with a 7-day history of slow response and unsteady walking, as reported by his family. Clinical features included impaired calculation skills, limited language expression, unresponsiveness, difficulty climbing stairs, inability to walk in a straight line, and irritability. No other symptoms such as weakness, numbness, fever, cough, diarrhea, headache, nausea, vomiting, altered consciousness, or convulsions were observed. Skin manifestations, such as resembling staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome or a diffuse erythema with superficial erosions, desquamation, and cheilitis resembling acrodermatitis enteropathica, were not found in our patient. The patient had an unremarkable medical and developmental history, and his relatives did not exhibit similar symptoms. However, his scholastic performance was notably poor compared to his peers, having completed only the 8th grade. Neurological examination revealed delayed reaction times, impaired calculation ability, significant dysmetria on heel–knee–shin testing, and a positive Romberg test. Plasma total homocysteine was 296.90 μmol/L (normal value 0.0 ~ 15.0 μmol/L) and D-dimer was 9.38 ng/mL (normal value 0.0 ~ 0.55 ng/mL), both elevated. Auxiliary examinations, including blood routine, biochemistry, thyroid function, rheumatic immune-related antibodies, folic acid, vitamin B12 concentrations, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and autoimmune encephalitis antibody examination, all yielded normal results.
A 24-year-old African woman was admitted to the hospital for a femoral neck fracture following a fall on the stairs. Surgical fixation was planned.

A 71-year-old female reported experiencing itchy lesions on the left side of her body that began 2 months prior. Upon physical examination, there were violet-colored, polygonal papules arranged along specific lines on the left side, including the left leg and arm. The patient has been on olanzapine for 2 years for schizophrenia. Examination of the mucous membranes and nails showed no abnormalities.
A 70-year-old male presented with a single pinkish nodule located on the back of his right hand. The patient reported no symptoms such as itching or pain.
A 59-year-old woman (patient no. 18196) presented with a history of progressive recession of the frontal hairline and loss of eyebrows since 2010.

The patient is a 9-year-old female child admitted to AVBR Hospital with an ear deformity and a short, deviated neck present since birth. She was born to parents who are not related by blood. The pregnancy was without complications, and there was no history of drug use or exposure to radiation. Her birth was uncomplicated, and there were no issues during or after delivery. She has developed normally. Her height is 119 cm, which is below the 3rd percentile for her age. On examination, her vital signs were stable. The right ear was malformed and lacked a visible vestibular canal, while the left ear had discharge. The neck was short and deviated to the right. There was kyphoscoliosis of the thoracic vertebrae. The right eye was smaller than the left and intermittently decreased in size involuntarily. Systemic examinations revealed abducens and right facial nerve palsy. An ophthalmic evaluation indicated retraction of the right eyeball.

A 32-year-old male farmer presented with recurrent swelling on the right side of the maxilla, persisting for six years. He had previously undergone surgery for a condition affecting the maxilla. The swelling extended through the skin and into the right nostril. Intraorally, the left maxilla was absent, and the teeth in the right maxilla were mobile, indicating involvement of the entire maxilla.

A 13-year-old boy was admitted in September 2018 due to severe respiratory distress and a global motor deficit, with the lower limbs more affected than the upper limbs. He exhibited motor regression, axial hypotonia with poor head control, muscle strength of 2–3/5 on the Medical Research Council’s scale (MRC) for the upper limbs, and 2/5 on the MRC scale for the lower limbs. There was generalized severe muscular atrophy and retractions of the elbow and knees, more pronounced in the distal segments. The patient was born from a non-consanguineous twin pregnancy at term without hypoxic events and has a healthy 19-year-old brother. In his first year, he was hypotonic with moderate motor delay, sitting after 1 year and walking without support after 2 years. He never achieved running, climbing stairs, or jumping on one foot, with the lower limbs consistently more affected than the upper limbs.

A 5-year-old Iranian boy presented with speech difficulties, lack of concentration, walking disability at age 4 leading to quadriplegia, spontaneous laughing and crying, clumsiness, psychomotor delay, and vision deterioration at age 5.

A 67-year-old Indian male presented with an itchy rash on the lower back for 10 days. He also observed pigmented rashes in both axillae and the left inframammary area of his chest. He had no prior history of skin rash or drug allergies. His medical history included hypertension for the past eight years, managed with telmisartan. Three months prior, his ophthalmologist noted left head tilt associated with right eye hypertropia when his head was straightened. Eye examination revealed fatigable ptosis of both eyelids with a positive Cogan’s lid twitch sign.

A 29-year-old female presented with recurrent episodes of slurred speech and right limb weakness lasting 1-3 hours, which began abruptly at 5 a.m. on the day prior to admission. These episodes occurred three times before progressing to persistent speech difficulties and complete paralysis of the right limbs by 1 p.m. on the day of admission.

DM is a 5-year-old male who first visited the Yale-New Haven Pediatric Clinic between the ages of 2 and 3 years old with delayed gross motor milestones and difficulty getting into a standing position. There was no family history of neurologic, developmental, or muscle diseases, and no evidence of consanguinity. His pregnancy and birth history were normal. Physical examination revealed prominent calves and forearms, an awkward gait, and poor running ability. He arose from the floor in a slow, stiff manner, but without the classical Gower’s sign. He could jump, climb stairs, and get into a chair without difficulty. Muscle strength was good, tone was normal, reflexes were brisk, and flexor plantar responses were present. Sensation, fine motor skills, vision, hearing, and cranial nerves were intact. CK level was 175 (24-195).
A 58-year-old woman presented in December 2018 with a mass in her right leg and a lesion in the right superficial lobe of the parotid gland.

A 4-year-old boy, born to nonconsanguineous parents and with normal developmental milestones, presented with drooping of both eyelids for 1 year. There was minimal fluctuation throughout the day, but symptoms worsened with exertion. Neurological examination revealed bilateral asymmetric ptosis and limited movement of the extraocular muscles, with minimal signs of fatigue upon exertion. Pupillary light reflex was normal. There was significant weakness in the finger extensors. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced. The remainder of the neurological examination was unremarkable. No skeletal deformities were observed, and there was no relevant family history. The neostigmine test was negative, and serum AChR antibodies were absent.

A 28-year-old female presented for a comprehensive eye examination in October 2019 at the Eye Clinic of the University of Campania L. Vanvitelli. She reported experiencing a gradual decrease in visual sharpness over the past few months. The patient has a history of myoclonic epilepsy accompanied by muscle weakness and significant motor impairment, which began around the age of 13.

A 46-year-old Caucasian female reported experiencing generalized hair loss over the past nine months, which had progressively worsened. She had no neurological or ophthalmological issues. Her medical history included Graves' disease and atrial fibrillation, with no record of inflammatory skin conditions.
